questions.q: What is the main difference between a process's log file and its execution report?
options: The log file is a technical, internal record of the process's steps; the report is a human-readable summary of the business outcome, like rows succeeded and rejected
There is no difference — they are the same file with two names
The log file only exists for ADFdi, never for FBDI
The report always contains less detail than the log in every case
questions.explain: The log captures internal, technical process detail. The report is built for a human reviewing what happened to the actual data — counts and rejection reasons.

questions.q: Why is a report showing '980 succeeded, 20 rejected' with no further detail less useful than one that lists each rejected row and its reason?
options: It isn't less useful — the numbers alone are always sufficient
Because without identifying which rows failed and why, there is no way to trace and fix the specific problems behind the 20 rejections
Because bigger numbers are always better regardless of detail
Because Oracle requires a minimum font size on every report
questions.explain: A useful report doesn't just report a count — it identifies which rows failed and the reason, which is what makes the rejections actionable.

questions.q: How do you find the output (report and log) for a specific process run among many others?
options: It's impossible to find a specific run's output
Ask a different user to email you a copy
Always open the very first process listed, regardless of date
Use the process name, submission time, and filters in Scheduled Processes to locate the exact run before opening its output
questions.explain: Scheduled Processes lets you identify the specific run by name, time, and submitting user — opening the wrong run's output risks drawing the wrong conclusion.

questions.q: A report shows zero rejected rows, but fewer total rows were processed than expected. What should you check?
options: Nothing — a zero-rejection report always means everything is fine
Only the ADFdi installer
The log file, which can reveal that rows were dropped earlier in the pipeline before the import process ever saw them
The UCM account name, which has no bearing on row counts
questions.explain: Rows dropped before reaching the interface table never appear as a 'rejection' in the import report — the log file is where that kind of earlier-stage loss can be traced.

questions.q: Which output should you typically check FIRST when reviewing the outcome of a completed import process?
options: The execution report, since it's built specifically to summarize the business outcome
The UCM account list
The original Excel template file
A coworker's unrelated process log
questions.explain: For day-to-day review, the execution report is the first stop; the log file becomes useful when the report alone doesn't explain something unexpected.
